#1421. Players we can’t believe were never sent off after James Tarkowski’s first Premier League red

James Tarkowski picked up the first red of his Premier League career on Monday night and let’s be honest, we all thought he had more than that.

Tarkowski was shown the red for the follow-through on a tackle on Brentford’s Yehor Yarmolyuk which saw his name crossed off a list of players who have surprisingly never received a red.

A career of 323 games and not a single red card is an impressive feat from King.

The former Tottenham defender’s struggles with injuries are well known with him only twice playing more than 30 Premier League games in a single season but when he was on the pitch, he was as composed as can be.

Not only did King never get his marching orders, he only got nine yellows in every match he played.

King’s numbers are impressive, but the record belongs to Hughes.

The former Newcastle, Fulham and Aston Villa man played 455 Premier League matches but never received a red card.

In total, the Northern Irishman played 675 games in his career and was never sent off, earning 19 yellows in that time.

Considering how composed he often looked, perhaps we could not be too surprised that Lahm features on this list.

He played in eight different positions in his career but never once was so out of his depth that he got himself sent off.

Lahm primarily operated as a full-back with 269 appearances on the right and 219 on the left before Pep Guardiola converted him into a defensive midfielder.

He did quite like a yellow though, getting 49 in his career.

Considering he played the majority of his career as a sweeper, it is particularly impressive that Italian legend Scirea was never sent off.

The World Cup and European Cup-winning defender played 621 times and yet was never given his marching orders.

To make it even more impressive, in his long career, which featured 551 games for Juventus, Scirea got just four yellow cards.

The former Match of the Day host is well known for having not only never received a red, but never even got booked either.

Lineker played 468 games, the majority of which were in the First Division, and yes he was a striker but we could show you a long list of number nines who have picked up a red.

The closest Lineker ever came was in Euro 1992 when he stamped on Basile Boli’s toe. The ref missed it and the pre-VAR world meant Lineker was in the clear.

Not only did Barnes never receive a red, but he was also the first player to make it past 100 Premier League games without a card of either colour.

Barnes played most of his football pre-Premier League, getting 349 appearances in the old First Division before making 201 in the Premier League, but never got a red.

He ended his career with 696 games played and not a single entry in the referee’s book.

Iniesta getting a red card just feels wrong, doesn’t it? Well, the good news is it’s never happened.

Iniesta played 885 games in his career, 674 of which were for Barcelona, but never received a red card.

He did pick up a fair few yellows, having got 74 in his time.

Considering he was quite a robust winger, Duff being on this list is surprising.

He played 629 games, starting off with Blackburn before moving to Chelsea in 2003, yet never got a red card.

Instead, he got 42 yellows, the majority of which came with Rovers, but he was largely a clean player.

#1415. The making of O Fenomeno: How Ronaldo became a global superstar at PSV

How do you even begin to choose your favourite version of Ronaldo Nazario?

The prodigy at Cruzeiro? The unstoppable force of nature at Bobby Robson’s Barcelona? The Galactico at Real Madrid? The heartbreak of France 98, the glorious redemption of the 2002 World Cup or the pre-injury sensation at Inter, when he looked destined to become the greatest striker of all time?

He even had his moments in a brief, mostly forgettable stint at AC Milan before rounding out his career with yet more silverware at Corinthians.

Over time, Ronaldo’s physique famously changed dramatically, his game evolved and the freakish acceleration that once made him impossible to catch was compromised by injuries. He suffered serious knee injuries, underwent multiple operations and had to rebuild his career more than once.

Younger generations can spend hours watching Ronaldo highlights on YouTube and still miss something fundamental about his greatness. The goals, the skills and the trademark explosive bursts are all there, but clips can’t capture the resilience that became such a defining part of his legend.

Kylian Mbappe is the obvious modern reference point, stylistically speaking: no other player is blessed with that devastating combination of pace, dynamism and finishing.

But mercifully, the French superstar has been spared the harrowing injuries that repeatedly threatened Ronaldo’s career. Mbappe is yet to experience the extraordinary highs and lows, the adversity and the comebacks, that made Ronaldo’s story so compelling.

In many ways, you can trace the whole arc of Ronaldo’s career back to his two seasons with PSV.

The jaw-dropping athleticism, the insane rate of goalscoring, the sense that defenders were powerless to stop him – it was all there for a teenager in his first stint in Europe. So, too, was the first major injury setback, the beginning of a long and painful relationship with the treatment table.

Ronaldo arrived in Eindhoven in 1994 as a 17-year-old, fresh from being part of Brazil’s World Cup-winning squad, albeit without playing a minute.

It might seem an unlikely destination for South America’s hottest prospect, but the European football landscape was unrecognisable if you view it through a modern lens.

This was an era in which arguably the best forward in the world – Romario – had stayed in Eindhoven for five full seasons. Meanwhile, over in Amsterdam, Louis van Gaal was building the best team on the planet. Ajax won the Champions League in 1994-95; Ronaldo’s PSV were competing with one of the great teams of that era.

Ajax were the dominant force in Dutch football, built around an outstanding collective rather than one superstar. They had exceptional players, of course, but nobody quite like Ronaldo.

The teenager hit the ground running at PSV, scoring one and setting up another on his Eredivisie debut before proceeding to take the league by storm.

PSV were a different proposition altogether. They lacked their great rivals’ cohesion and tactical sophistication, and they made a chaotic start to that campaign.

A hat-trick from Ronaldo couldn’t prevent PSV from losing 5-4 to Bayer Leverkusen in an early-season UEFA Cup qualifier; an apt reflection of where that team was at.

“The Ronaldo show started, and he scored three goals,” former PSV Technical Director Frank Arnesen later told Mundial.

“But it wasn’t about the goals even; there was one detail in the game that was incredible. He received the ball in his own half. The ball is played to him, and the German right back assaults him from behind in a dangerous way.

“He lifts the ball with the outside of his left shoe, around the defender, and jumps. Ronaldo passes him by on the other side and starts a solo. He moves past three or four men, one man two times. Then all of Europe knew about Ronaldo.”

﻿

While Ronaldo was swiftly establishing himself as the most exciting talent of his generation, PSV were struggling to keep pace. Manager Aad de Mos had bafflingly deployed centre-forward Erik Meijer at left-back in the defeat to Leverkusen and departed in October.

Kees Rijvers stepped in on a caretaker basis before Dick Advocaat was eventually appointed in December, making for a turbulent introduction to life in Europe.

The Farmers – the club’s nickname, but not an entirely unfair reflection of their level – finished third, behind Roda JC and a full 14 points adrift of Van Gaal’s unbeaten Ajax side in 1994-95.

That gap would have been even greater under the three-points-for-a-win system. Still, in an otherwise struggling PSV side, Ronaldo was a class apart, claiming the Golden Boot with 30 Eredivisie goals – 12 more than his nearest challenger, fellow wonderkid Patrick Kluivert.

The buck-toothed teenager was doing that all that while adapting to life on a new continent, experiencing the culture shock of his first winter in the chilly, damp industrial heartland of the Netherlands.

It was there and then that he learned to drive, with his instructor recalling him in the glowing tones of a proud youth coach speaking to The Athletic for a long read.

“His driving skills were excellent, of course, but his scanning, his awareness of his surroundings, and his anticipation, the things we actually train for, were far from elite-level,” John Dekker told Dutch outlet omroepbrabant, with a nod to his student’s newfound celebrity status.

“It was incredible how quickly people recognised him. People crowding around the car, girls sitting on the hood… it was great fun.”

PSV were an entertaining side, but the real improvements came after a full pre-season under Advocaat. By the start of 1995-96, they looked a considerably more coherent outfit, with Ronaldo leading an increasingly formidable attack. They were routinely running riot domestically, putting four, five, seven and even eight goals past Eredivisie opponents.

@Inter_en @Ronaldo Sorry, but we’re not convinced 😜

O Fenomeno looked set to go truly stratospheric when he scored four goals and set up another two as PSV demolished Finnish minnows MyPa 7-1, a performance that bordered on bullying.

Yet the Dutch side had plenty of other weapons. Ronaldo sat out their 5-3 win over Leeds at Elland Road and wasn’t among the scorers in the 3-0 home victory in the second leg. There was no repeat of the previous season’s debacle as they cruised through qualifying into the UEFA Cup proper.

But just as things were gathering pace, Ronaldo suffered his first major injury: a patellar tendon tear that kept him sidelined for almost the entire second half of the season, including a minor UEFA Cup classic against Barcelona. PSV gave the Catalans two terrific games but ultimately bowed out 5-4 on aggregate in the quarter-finals.

Who knows what Advocaat’s PSV might have gone on to achieve had they kept their one bonafide superstar fit and available? They finished runners-up that season, closing the gap to just six points on an Ajax side that Van Gaal had led to a second successive Champions League final.

Ronaldo returned towards the end of the campaign, but not without conflict. His relaxed Brazilian temperament didn’t always sit comfortably with Advocaat’s strict Dutch sensibilities, echoing the coach’s issues with Gullit. Ronaldo reportedly called his manager an “idiot” after being left out of the starting XI for the KNVB Cup final.

“Yes, he did say that,” Advocaat later confirmed.

“Ronaldo was out injured for a long time in his second year. We used Rene Eijkelkamp in his place. When Ronaldo recovered, he demanded to start in the Cup final against Sparta. I didn’t want to take the risk, and he got very angry and said some harsh words. But we had no lasting problems.”

“At times, I felt like a father to him. After away games, he’d fall asleep on the bus with his head resting on my shoulder. He was open and had his personal struggles, but to me, he was a sweet kid.”

Ronaldo was introduced from the bench for a late cameo and promptly notched an assist, adding extra gloss to a 5-2 victory. He had his trophy, giving him a fitting send-off in his final appearance.

There would be considerably more spectacular comebacks in the years ahead. While the knee injury was an early warning of what was to come, it hadn’t yet taken anything away from Ronaldo’s extraordinary physical gifts.

At Barcelona the following season, he reached arguably the highest level of his career, described by Spanish football lifer Sid Lowe as “quite possibly the best, most freakishly brilliant thing I have ever seen.”

The 2002 World Cup is the obvious Oscar-bait centrepiece for a Ronaldo biopic. His PSV years would be the indie arthouse prequel: A human story of teenage brilliance, growing pains and the fighter behind the phenomenon. The connoisseur’s choice for a favourite Ronaldo chapter.

#1411. Elite players with a terrible penalty record as Lamine Yamal misses another one

Lamine Yamal missed another penalty at the weekend, meaning he has missed more than he has scored this season, but he is not the only elite player with a pretty poor record.

Yamal failed to convert from the spot when Barcelona were trailing 2-0 to Villarreal and even if his blushes were spared thanks to his teammates, it still added to his mixed bag of a penalty record.

Yamal has scored 11 and missed three, giving him a success rate of 79% and here are 10 other elite players who are not so great from the penalty spot.

Messi used to be absolutely awful at penalties. He missed four in the 2014-15 season and did so again in both of the following campaigns. No wonder he tried passing the ball rather than shooting.

Typical of Messi, he clearly identified it as a weakness and worked to improve it. He missed just one a season for the following two campaigns and is now one of the best penalty takers.

His earlier career form does though mean he still makes this list.

Griezmann would choose to have missed 100 penalties if he scored that one in Milan.

The former Atletico man missed a penalty during the Champions League final against city rivals Madrid in the San Siro, a match his team would go on to lose.

Griezmann did at least score in the penalty shootout but could have given Atletico a great chance at victory in the 90 minutes.

That was one of 14 penalties missed in his career to date.

For a player who seemed able to do pretty much whatever he wanted with the ball, Mahrez was oddly poor when it came to penalties.

He’s missed 12 in total, including four for both Leicester and Manchester City.

If you are looking for a player to have missed a penalty for a lot of different clubs, then Edin Dzeko is your man.

He’s missed spot kicks for five clubs and another for his international team, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

He only ever took one for City and missed it before Sergio Aguero resumed duties and his stint at Fenerbahce saves him from a frankly embarrassing record.

He managed to score seven for the Turkish club, missing two, which rescues him somewhat.

Ribery took eight penalties in the 2007-08 season alone but managed to miss two of them.

After that, he was never really given a first-choice run at spot kicks and only took three more for Bayern.

He did have a 100% record for France, though.

The Pro Evo 6 cheat code may have been able to blast them at will from 30 yards but it was not so easy from 12.

He missed a third of the ones he took, of which the majority came whilst he was at Inter.

Had his career ended there, then his penalty record would have been awful but he did redeem himself somewhat with nine scored and one missed for Flamengo in his latter career.

Missing more penalties than you have scored definitely means you are worth including on this list.

Sterling has failed to score six of the 10 penalties he has scored, so no wonder he was taken off penalty duty.

He scored his first-ever penalty back in the 2017-18 season but then missed the next two he took.

Sterling left City with a record of three scored and four missed but was somehow even worse for Chelsea and Arsenal. He took one for each London club and missed both of them.

A 232-goal striker should make for a prolific penalty taker, right? Wrong.

Inzaghi was surprisingly bad from spot kicks, even if he was only given a limited opportunity to take them.

The former Juventus and Milan player only took 25 in his long career and perhaps that is because he missed eight of them.

Most of his misses came from Milan where he scuffed three and managed to score two. No wonder then he took his final penalty nine years before the end of his career.

At one point in his career, Isak was awful at penalties.

When he left Spain for Newcastle in 2022, he had scored six but missed four and since coming to England he has improved a lot.

He missed one in the 2023-24 Premier League season and another in a UEFA Nations League match for Sweden but has scored 13 in the same time period.

His earlier work does mean he has a bad record, for now.

Vinicius Junior took over Cristiano Ronaldo’s number seven shirt but clearly did not inherit his penalty-taking ability.

Of the 20 he has taken, Vinicius has missed six. His most recent came in the 2025/26 Champions League and since then, Kylian Mbappe has been Madrid’s first-choice penalty taker.

Ronaldo, by comparison, has a conversion record of 83%.

#1409. 8 naff football-related presents you could get this Christmas: Soap, Cards, Monopoly…

It’s getting close to that time of year when your relatives know you like football and so try their best to get a gift, but they don’t always quite get it right.

Liking football means you often get just about anything as a gift provided it has your club’s badge on it (if you’re lucky) and let’s all hope that none of us open any of these under the tree this year.

Here are eight wonderfully awful football-related Christmas gifts for this year.

When we heard Bristol City were selling grass we thought that’s one way to raise the transfer budget but turns out it is of the turf variety.

The Robins are releasing soap that has been “scientifically” made to replicate the smell of the pitch at Ashton Gate so you can shower with the smell of a pitch that is 18th in the Championship currently.

We will give them credit for the excellent slogan of “because you’re turf it” but it has naturally opened them to such jokes as it smelling like the s**t football that gets played on it.

Profits will at least go to the club’s foundation.

Introducing the Ashton Gate-scented soap to raise funds for the Robins Foundation’s work in communities across Bristol.

Available online and in-store. https://t.co/kbDyZ1XbTC

— Bristol City FC (@BristolCity) November 24, 2026

Ipswich are selling a Christmas candle called Ipswicks which they describe as a Luxury Scented Christmas Candle smelling of Pine, Eucalyptus & Cedarwood.

We don’t know what the Ipswich marketing department thinks of their fans though as there is a warning to not touch the tin as it may get hot.

Club-branded playing cards is not that unusual but we are including these because Arsenal have decided to charge their fans £70 for three packs of cards.

For that money, you get a commemorative box that has the names of the players that won the title last season and the cards are in the colours of the kits used last campaign but we hope no one buys that because that is an incredible waste of money.

Just imagine, you’ve had your Christmas dinner and someone suggests some card games and then pulls those out. Awful.

If you think £70 is too much, then don’t worry, you can get a single pack of cards for £18.

Honestly, there are so many things from the United store that could have made the list. Firstly, they are selling quite literally a cardboard box for £10. They also have a sack so the jokes write themselves.

But the one item we have picked out is the United-branded Monopoly board they are selling for £50.

Realising that there are not 28 United-related places to go on a Monopoly board, the club decided to name each square after moments in their history, fair enough. What isn’t fair enough is that the final square, which is the most expensive slot on the board, comes with the title of “2016/17 WON THE LOT.”

Sorry? We’ve checked the league table and can’t help but see you were sixth? And surely the FA have made a mistake because they seem to think that Arsenal won the cup that year? While we are at it, you will want to have a word with UEFA because they seem to think that Real Madrid won the Champions League that season.

“The lot” United are referring to is actually the League Cup, Europa League and Community Shield. Did Jose Mourinho commission this?

Well they’ve got to pay their massive wages somehow.

Man Utd truly shocking in 2026-27 Premier League wage bill vs. position comparison

It may have slipped your attention but did you know that League Two side Northampton Town are now owned by a Brazilian consortium fronted by Alexandre Pato?

#1408. Premier League table vs squad cost 2026-27: Man Utd are the biggest underachievers…

We are 11 games into the Premier League season. Who are the biggest underperformers and overachievers? Manchester United and Hull City, in particular, make for an interesting contrast when you compare their league position with how much their squads cost to assemble.

While squad cost is not a direct assessment of how a team should perform, it does give us an idea of where they should be aiming for.

With that in mind, we’ve taken the current Transfermarkt valuation of each Premier League squad cost and compared it to where each team currently finds itself in the table.

And boy, does it make Manchester United look bad. United are 19th in the Premier League table, despite having the fifth-most expensive squad in the division, giving them a 14-place disparity between their squad cost position and their actual league position.

That’s miles worse than even the likes of Newcastle and Chelsea, who this table doesn’t exactly make pretty reading for either.

At the other end of the scale, Everton are seventh despite having the 16th-most expensive squad in the division. That puts them nine places above where their squad cost would suggest they might be expected to be.

Leeds are also punching well above their weight, sitting sixth despite ranking 17th for squad cost. That’s a difference of +11. Hull are 11th despite having the cheapest squad in the division, putting them nine places above their squad cost ranking.

Brighton (+7), Bournemouth (+6), Coventry (+5) and Arsenal (+5) have also outperformed their squad cost rankings.

Manchester City, meanwhile, are third in the Premier League while having the second-most expensive squad according to Transfermarkt.

#1407. A tribute to Dean Ashton, the best striker England never had

After shining for Norwich City and West Ham, Dean Ashton became one of England’s big hopes, but a combination of factors meant we never saw the best of the striker for the Three Lions. It’s a sad ‘what if’ story.

Every time an England squad is announced for a major tournament, we get the inevitable complaints about certain players missing the cut, albeit for different reasons.

Occasionally we’ll see complaints that the squad gets packed with established names at the expense of exciting youngsters, while at other times we’ll wind up with younger players from top clubs making the cut ahead of in-form talents from less-fancied clubs.

The latter was certainly the complaint of many when Theo Walcott made the squad for the 2006 World Cup ahead of Darren Bent coming off the back of an impressive season with Charlton.

But there was another player who could feel hard done by: Dean Ashton.

Being overlooked was a recurring theme. In fact, you have to wonder how many more of those predicted future England XIs – which brought notoriety to the likes of Dean Parrett and Patrick Roberts – he’d have featured in had he come through the ranks of a top club’s academy rather than Crewe’s, which was still known for producing top talents but certainly not at the same rate as in the 90s.

However, those who saw him in the early part of his career can attest he was always a special talent.

Indeed, after he left the Cheshire club for Norwich in January 2005 with them in the top half of the Championship, they proceeded to go 18 games without a win and only stayed up on the final day of the season.

Even then, aged just 21, he looked as close as you could get to the complete striker, scoring 20 in 27 games for the Alex and adding seven for a struggling Canaries side after making his top-flight bow.

That tally included a quite lovely volley against Manchester City, the finish of a young man who felt he couldn’t fail with anything he attempted.

Looking at Ashton, most would never have identified him as a man capable of such subtlety, but a lot of that can be put down to England’s specific record with players of his ilk.

The Three Lions have often resisted demanding too much of their frontmen: either giving them the ‘Big man up top’ responsibilities or ensuring they’re nippy with tidy finishing ability – as if anticipating every single pairing should be modelled on the platonic ideal of Niall Quinn and Kevin Phillips.

In fact, going all-in on a combo that was happy with some nice moments and a seventh-place finish does seem quite England, on reflection.

Anyway, by tempering expectations, the sight of a more complete frontman has tended to confuse people, leading to Ashton – even off the back of another great season in 2005-06, overlooked for that summer’s World Cup in Germany.

Indeed, when Walcott was handed a surprise call-up having played no first-team football since January that season, Darren Bent – not Ashton – was the man who many said should feel hard-done-by.

But while not as prolific as some in that half-season, Ashton was capable of scoring goals you wouldn’t back others to produce – not least his clincher in the FA Cup quarter-final win over Manchester City.

The sight of a hefty striker dancing through a defence with grace and tidy footwork is an underrated genre of goal, like a bear performing ballet, and this was on par with Johan Elmander doing the same for Bolton a few years later.

It showed Ashton had that touch of class needed to unlock bunched defences, and – with fitness question marks around some of the other squad members that summer – it’s very easy to make retrospective demands for his inclusion with the benefit of a decade’s distance.

Of course, Ashton’s fitness in the summer of 2006 would almost prove ironic given the struggles later in his career, beginning with his first England call-up not long after that World Cup.

An injury in training, following a challenge from Shaun Wright-Phillips, ended up being one from which he never fully recovered, though there was one more hot season – and one stand-out goal – to celebrate before his early retirement in 2009 at the age of just 26.

Ashton’s consolation goal in West Ham’s May 2008 defeat to Manchester United was to overhead kicks what Ashton himself was to No.9s: very different to what we’ve come to expect from the genre, but that doesn’t mean it doesn’t work.

Overhead kicks, generally speaking, can be divided into the Rivaldo-style self-assisted efforts and the side-on excellence produced by the likes of Eidur Gudjohnsen for Chelsea against Leeds United.

Ashton’s was neither of these things, yet the ugly beauty of the finish was a sight to behold.

Ashton eyes up the ball like a sniper keeping sight of a moving target, but the process is complicated by his own continued need to readjust. And yet, with the close attentions of Rio Ferdinand and the looming sight of Edwin van der Sar, not once did he seem to consider the prospect of not making a clean contact on the ball.

Would it have been easier to go for a header? Yes. Would it have been more efficient to bring the ball down and beat Van der Sar that way? Almost certainly. Would we be talking about the goal if he’d done either of those things? Heavens no.

Sadly for Ashton, whose one England cap would come that summer, that was pretty much the end of it. He managed just a handful of games the following season before his ankle flared up once more and he made the difficult decision to walk away from the game.

Had England qualified for that summer’s European Championships, he might have been given his chance at a major tournament.

But then again, a healthy Dean Ashton might itself have been enough for England to qualify in the first place.

With England misfiring on more than one occasion in tournaments, conversations invariably turn towards those who played and failed to score. But perhaps we should be talking about the missing piece of the jigsaw who wasn’t there.

#1406. Tuur Rommens eyes a strong home run for Rangers that can set platform for a title tilt

Published: 12:40 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 12:40 EST, 22 November 2026

Tuur Rommens has urged his Rangers team-mates to use a breakneck run of three home games in eight days to build a platform from which to launch a real assault on the Premiership title.

Derek McInnes’ side play host to Aberdeen on Tuesday and then have Falkirk and Dundee United visiting – with Belgian left-back Rommens clear on the need to use the Ibrox atmosphere as a weapon.

‘At the away games, there’s a lot of fans, but at home there’s even more, so it gives an extra boost,’ he said.

‘I think, at home, we have to maintain our good run.

‘We’ll try to keep on winning these three games and then we’ll see from there. If you keep winning, you’ll be up there.

‘We’re back to Ibrox (on Tuesday) and it’s been a long time, but, yeah, it’s nice to play in front of our fans again.

Tuur Rommens (right) celebrates with match-winner Ryan Naderi at Fir Park

Emmanuel Fernandez headed home the opener in Rangers' 2-1 victory at Motherwell

‘I guess Aberdeen, it’s a difficult one, but we’ll try to keep on winning.’

Rangers dug out a crucial 2-1 win at Motherwell on Saturday thanks to an 88th-minute Ryan Naderi winner and sit four points behind leaders Celtic with a game in hand.

Rommens believes the side’s ability to pull wins out of the fire and show they are willing to keep pushing right to the end of matches is helping build unity within the squad and with their followers.

‘Yeah, exactly,’ he said. ‘Also with the fans, when you score you feel a lot of emotions. You feel that they’re so happy, we’re so happy, so it gives us extra boost to go on Tuesday again and try to get a win.

‘I think the fanbase is unbelievable. It doesn’t feel like an away game because there are so many fans with us.

‘Especially for the new guys, that’s new. It’s the same for me. I’m not even here one year so I’m getting surprised every time that there are so many fans of Rangers when we’re playing outside.’

Rommens also took time to lavish praise on Naderi and revealed what a deeply loved figure the Czech international has become within the dressing room.

Asked about the progress Naderi has made with his game in recent months, he replied: ‘It’s unbelievable.

‘You can always give the ball to him and he just keeps it.

‘He’s very strong and I think he deserves all these goals that he gets. So yeah, I’m very happy for him.

‘He delivers, he scores a lot of goals, he gives assists, so everybody’s happy for him and he’s a good guy. Everybody loves him in the group.’

#1405. Rangers must find their shooting boots quicker to prevent the need to dig themselves out of needless holes

Published: 12:52 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 13:26 EST, 22 November 2026

Derek McInnes chose to dress up the poor level of chance conversion from his Rangers side as something for those insistent on dwelling on the negatives at the end of a last-gasp win over Motherwell.

That’s fair enough. He wants to keep the energy up. He wants to place the focus, instead, on a 13-game unbeaten run. He wants to make more of the fact his team are capable of digging in and getting wins over the line by hook or by crook even when it isn’t going exactly to plan.

It’s a form of motivation, and motivating people doesn’t always come through hammering on about their deficiencies. The truth is this, though: you really shouldn’t be needing a scrappy 88th-minute winner courtesy of a couple of jammy deflections in a game which has seen you deliver 29 shots on goal with 11 of those on target.

Yes, Motherwell keeper Alex Paulsen had a good night. One double save from substitute Findlay Curtis and Dujon Sterling in the 85th minute was quite exceptional. This, however, wasn’t quite the superhuman display from the Kiwi that many were making it out to be.

A lot of the saves he made were straightforward. Too often, Rangers blazed efforts high and wide. They dominated the first quarter of this game until Jake Girdwood-Reich cancelled out Manny Fernandez’s early opener, lost their rhythm a bit, as they are wont to do, and then ran the show completely in the second half.

They should have won by a country mile and it is necessary to look into why they didn’t.

Ryan Naderi rejoices in scoring Rangers' late winner against Motherwell

Emmanuel Fernandez broke the deadlock on eight minutes at Fir Park

McInnes was justified in being happy with many aspects of his side’s performance at Fir Park. Ryan Naderi did put in a strong display as he spearheaded the frontline, although he did miss two gilt-edged chances before settling it late on with an untidy effort that deflected off Martin Moormann — who had already blocked a Badredine Bouanani shot — and landed in the net.

The Czech international is developing a reputation for important goals that are getting Rangers out of the mire — and keeping them in contention for the title — but McInnes needs infinitely more in terms of numbers from those around him.

Not xG or pass completion or any of those niche interests. Goals and assists is what we’re talking about here. The stuff that really changes games and puts points on the board.

First in the dock on this front, talented individuals that really need to be held to account, are attackers Minsu Kim and Bouanani. Listen, McInnes has already spoken plenty on the need for both of them to deliver more in those key metrics. He obviously doesn’t want to come across as a stuck record.

Both players are technically proficient. They are exciting. The view from this vantage point is that they very definitely do have it in them to be gamechangers, but they’re starting to get a little bit annoying now.

Thanks to the corner that set up Fernandez for the opening goal, Minsu, who started in a more central role with Kevin Kelsy being benched, does have one assist on the board finally. That’s a pretty grim return, though, from 15 appearances.

Particularly worrying from the South Korean was his reaction when presented with a golden opportunity to break his scoring duck just before the hour. Naderi teed him up perfectly with a pass to the left. Minsu had time to control the ball and pick his spot.

His sclaffed effort, easily saved by Paulsen at the near post, was atrocious. It reeked of a guy short of confidence in the final third and growing progressively more anxious about getting his name on the scoresheet. Maybe he’s just trying too hard, but he needs to get the finger out, keep the mind calm and start taking the heat off the likes of Naderi and Kelsy with some major contributions.

Same goes for Bouanani. His late effort did, at least, lead to Naderi’s winner, albeit more through accident than design, but his record reads one goal and one assist in 10 appearances. He’s a dangerous, tricky winger. He beats people for fun. He should be doing more than this.

Djeidi Gassama, a more limited player than Minsu or Bouanani, started against Motherwell and does have five assists to his name, but he’s only managed one goal, in a 5-1 League Cup rout of St Mirren.

Meanwhile, Findlay Curtis has no goals and no assists from 15 outings, although only five of those have been first-team starts.

That’s four blokes who play along the frontline and they’ve managed two goals between them. You do the maths on that.

Derek McInnes was delighted at full-time but Rangers should have won with more comfort

There are others throughout the team, though, who can be doing more to make life easier from a goalscoring perspective.

Fernandez announced himself as a real threat from set-pieces last season. He’s a real weapon in the air. Saturday’s goal was his first this term. Rangers need to do better at harnessing what he brings in an attacking context from dead-ball situations.

A few more in the way of goal interventions from midfield would be welcome, too. Dan Neil can finish. He showed that with those two spectacular goals against Celtic in the 3-0 Premier Sports Cup win at Ibrox in September.

In his 17 other outings outwith that match, however, he has only scored once and delivered one assist. He had a brilliant chance at Fir Park just after the interval and slid it wide of the far post.

Nico Raskin, meanwhile, has one goal and no assists to his name.

He put one great chance from a header wide in the second half. Then he blazed over from a promising position after releasing Bouanani out wide with a super diagonal ball and running a ridiculous distance to latch onto the return.

McInnes insists he’s never seen a squad practise crossing and shooting like this one. However much they are doing in training at Auchenhowie, they need to bring it to matchdays.

Everything is there for Rangers this season. There are definitely promising signs in their overall play while Celtic, of course, are poorly run from a footballing perspective with an OAP manager, and a fanbase in open revolt against the board.

Rangers now have a run of six games from eight at home that could — and should — be a real platform for a serious title bid.

They just have to wake up to the fact that depending on Naderi to drag them out of a hole and drag them over the line again and again and again is simply not a sustainable way of working.

Motherwell (4-2-3-1): PAULSEN 8.5; Sparrow 7, Girdwood-Reich 7, Moormann 7, Longelo 6; Fadinger 6, Priestman 6; Maswanhise 6, Said 5 (Charles-Cook 15 (Kanga 63)), Hodge 5 (Bjorgolfsson 86); Palmer-Houlden 5 (Hendry 63). Booked: Hendry. Manager: Alfred Johansson 6.

Rangers (4-2-3-1): Pandur 7; Sterling 7, Fernandez 7, Makhanya 6, Rommens 6; Raskin 7, Neil 6.5 (Chukwuani 86); Bouanani 7, Minsu 6.5 (Curtis 78), Gassama 6 (Kelsy 69); Naderi 7.5. Booked: Naderi. Manager: Derek McInnes 7.

#1404. Man Utd impress in draw against PSG but injury worries mount

Michael Carrick said he had to be careful with Mason Mount after the England midfielder handed Manchester United an injury scare in their friendly draw with Paris St Germain.

Mount has had a torrid time with injuries since signing from Chelsea in a £55m-deal three years ago, starting only 25 Premier League games for United in that time.

The 27-year-old has been successfully deployed by Carrick in a central midfield role during pre-season, leading to speculation that United may not make another expected signing in that department.

But Mount played only 18 minutes of Saturday’s 1-1 draw against the European champions in Gothenburg before being replaced by Scotland international Tyler Fletcher.

“He [Mount] got kicked. We just wanted to be careful and look after him,” Carrick, the United head coach, told reporters in Sweden.

“We’ve been lucky with injuries so far, so we wanted to be careful.”

Post-match video footage showed Mount walking freely on to the United bus without the aid of a protective boot or knee support.

Michael Carrick told VG Mason Mount was taken off as a precaution. Looked OK leaving stadium. pic.twitter.com/Uo0fBtgpAl

United went behind within two minutes at the Ullevi Stadium when Liverpool target Ibrahim Mbaye punished slack marking to put PSG ahead.

Bryan Mbeumo fired United level after 32 minutes following good work from Amad Diallo, the Cameroon forward’s third goal in two games after his match-winning double against Atletico Madrid.

United meet Leeds in a Dublin friendly on Wednesday before coming up against AC Milan and their former manager Ruben Amorim next Saturday.

United open their Premier League campaign at Hull on August 22.

“It was good game. PSG is good so we had to keep building fitness. I am happy to have other [players] back and we have to keep going.”

“It’s good for me. I enjoyed it. We need to build fitness, we have a big season ahead.”

“It’s a good game PSG are tough to beat and we got a draw and now think about the next game [against Leeds in Dublin].”

“We have two more games against Leeds a and Milan. We need to have big season and hope to win a trophy.”

All over in Gothenburg and it’s been a good match for Michael Carrick’s team. They looked sharper and quicker than their win over Atletico Madrid last week (what the manager wanted) and things are moving in the right direction. Two things to worry about, however, were the early exits of Mason Mount and Tom Heaton with injuries. They’ll especially hope the Mount knock isn’t anything mid or long term.

Nearly done and it’s been a good run out for United. They’ve looked the better, sharper side and, if anything, deserve to win. In mitigation, this is United fourth pre-season game to PSG’s second...

Fernandes has one thing on his mind when he gets the ball 25 yards out in the centre of the park - a shot. He unleashes the attempt, destined for the bottom-left corner, forcing Longoni, the sub goalkeeper, into a good save.

Two chances for United in quick succession. A lovely ball from the middle of the park by Zirkzee finds Dalot on the right. He chips the ball to the back post where one of the Fletchers (sorry, I am not sure which) heads for goal. His attempt is blocked and the ball, ultimately, falls at the feet of Lacey whose shot is blazed high over the bar.

There have been plenty of good things for Carrick to take from this match. The passing, while not of the standard of a cut-and-thrust Premier League match, has been good for the time of year, and there have been enough flashes of brilliance/class/invention etc to suggest that pre-season is moving in the right direction.

Lovely bit of play by United. A great pass with the outside of the boot from the inside-left channel by Tielemans finds Fernandes who plays a sidefooted shot that goes just wide.

Tielemans’s first bit of brilliance from the Belgian there.

Both sides losing possession a fair bit at the moment. Strong pre-season vibes right now.

Maguire has had a good game. He’s played a number of long passes from the back and looked assured. This time he’s up in the PSG half and decides to have a pop - his shot testing Safanov, who saves well.

Had there been VAR Safanov might have had something to answer for...he may have beaten Zirkzee to the ball but he flew in the air and jurt the United man in the process.

Anwway, there’s no VAR (hurrah, for those of you who consider it a modern-day evil) and it doesn’t matter.

Chance for United to go ahead and it comes from two things. (i) A long, hopeful ball from Fernandes that looks for Zirkzee (ii) Safanov rushing off his line and into no-man’s land. The ball comes loose and Jack Fletcher, instead of having a go at goal, with the keeper on the ground and out of the game, passes to Lacey whose shot is wide.

Tyler Fletcher loses the ball near the United half and it, ultimately, results in a PSG corner. From the set piece United defend well and snuff out all hint of danger.

PSG seeing more of the ball at the moment. They work the ball to the right and Amass brings down Mbaye.

From the resulting free-kick, in the final third, the French side whip in the ball but Mee is up ot the challenge and come to collect well.

Santos, Mbeumo, Shaw, Amad, Lacey are off

Fernandes, Jack Feltcher, Zirkzee and Amass are on.

A raft of changes for PSG sees Marquinhos and João Neves, among others, come on. More like it, in terms of first-team ‘names’, on the pitch for the European Cup champions.

United on top in this half, as they were in the first.

The paces quickens and the game is much better for it. Mbuemo drives toward the PSG box, he cuts inside from the right before unleashing a shot that is bound for the back of the net before a fine one-handed save by Safanov. Credit, too, for Maguire whose long ball from the back found Mbuemo brilliantly. Promising...

Lacey tries to play in Dorgu on the left but he’s asking too much of his team-mate. Wonder when the expected raft of changes will take place?

Slow start to the second half. This is very much pre-season-friendly pace.

Having seen Mount limp off in the first half, there’s more worry at the start of the second and Heaton is force off with what looks like a hamstrung injury. He dashed off his line to clear a ball and in doing so has tweaked something. Mee replaces him.

Back under way Gothenburg - there have been a number of changes and will bring them to you once I’ve worked out who has come on and who they’ve replaced.

A world record that still stands...(this was back in 1995).

And that is it for the first 45 minutes. PSG took the early lead, but from that moment on United have been the better side and deservedly are level through Mbueno’s goal.

There will be one minute of added time at the end of what has been a good first half for Man Utd.

Amad has a go from outside the box forcing the save from Safanov. He’s such a live wire and one of the best in his position in the top flight. Him or Antony? No contest, strange it took United a while to work that one out.

Yet more good work from the underrated Amad. He again closes down well on the right before winning back possession and cutting the ball back for Lacey. To think he was starring for Sunderland in the Championship while Antony was starting for United...

United have been the better side since conceding earlier and, as if to illustrate my point, as I typed that an Mbuemo free-kick is well saved by Safanov. That was heading for the top-right bin.

Great work on the left by Dorgu and Shaw ends with the latter chipping the ball to the back post where Amad is lurking with intent. The Ivorian looks to head the ball home, but before he can get anything on it it looks as though he’s pushed in the back. United players are sure it’s a penalty but, more importantly, the referee doesn’t.

Amad does brilliantly, winning the ball off Koukaba in the final third, from there he scampers toward the box before playing in Mbuemo who takes one touch before firing in a shot into the bottom right corner of the net.

Free-kick for PSG on the right, near the final third. The ball comes in and it’s straight into the arms of Heaton in the United goal.

Kvaratskhelia, not seen much of him so far, runs into the box, but Amad does well to usher him back out.

The match is pedestrian at the moment, but as I type that, Dorgu, yep, him again, drives down the left and puts in a good cross that is well intercepted by Safanov in the PSG goal.

United continue to see more of the ball, Dorgu’s seeing more of it than most. But, no chances really fashioned, still, plenty of time to go.

Worry for United having to sub off Mount. It looks as though he took a knock to a foot and Carrick and co will hope it’s not a long-term injury. Mount, who’s had a good pre-season, has been replaced by Fletcher, son of Darren.

Foul on Mazraoui results in two things. The Mount has to come off, and, United have a free-kick on the edge of the PSG area.

From the set-piece Mbuemo has a go and it’s a regulation save from Safonov in the PSG goal.

Heaven loses possession in the middle of the park and from there it’s like the parting of the Red Sea as PSG have a three-on-one. Mbaye gets the shot in on goal but Andrey Santos covers back brilliantly and does enough to get something on the ball. He’s started both this match and pre-season well.

United are looking half decent on the ball. They’re passing it well and not afraid to switch things around.

A lovely long ball from Maguire finds Dorgo whose lovely first touch takes him into the box before a cut back is intercepted by a PSG man. Promising signs though for Carrick’s men.

United seeing more of the ball at the moment. They’re being patient but cannot fashion an opening and the ball is worked all the way back to Heaton in goal.

Needless to say this is being played at a slowish pace...no blood-and-guts challenges being put in.

Good work down the right sees Amad plays in Shay Lacey who crosses into the box. The ball find shte head of Mbuemo and the ball sails over the bar. Better from United.

United started slowly against Atletico and they’ve done the same here.

Bright start to say the least from the French side. They work the ball left and it’s an easy cross from Dro Fernandez for Mbaye to tap home for the very early lead.

They’re under way in Sweden. United are in their new vibrant red kit and PSG in their blue, red and white kit. Big fan of the French side’s kit, it harks back to the kit they had in the 1990s when the likes of George Weah and David Ginola were entertaining in the capital of France.

“Get a bit sharper, get better on the ball, go up a notch.”

“It’s not about today it’s about preparing. Some players have played 90 minutes, some have played three games, some have just come back. So it’s about keeping working on things we’ve been working on.”

A hugely talented player for a number of clubs, including United, who ever really lived up to his early promise.

I expect they’ll make an appearence at some point.

Ready to face PSG in our latest pre-season test ✊

Manchester United continue their Sweden sojourn with match against Paris St-Germain in Gothenburg.

Clearly a clash against the back-to-back Champions League winners is a step up from their previous two pre-season friendlies (victories against Rosenborg and Atletico Madrid), but at the same time this is more a chance for players to get miles in the legs and see how new signings and possibly some young guns fit in.

One of those new signings is Youri Tielemans, and the Belgian international is in line to make his debut after his move from Aston Villa. Other team news is that Bruno Fernandes is back and ready to captain the team.

Michael Carrick has also been boosted by the returns of Matheus Cunha, Diogo Dalot and Noussair Mazraoui after their post-World Cup breaks.

Cunha, however, will not play a part in today’s match because of a “minor illness” according to the MUTV website. He is expected to link up with the squad in Ireland, where they face Leeds United at Croke Park, after the match.

This will be Man Utd’s first outing since the 2-1 win over Atletico, a performance and result that pleased Carrick.

“I enjoyed it, I thought there was a lot of good in things that we are looking to improve on,” the United manager said. “Building on what we did for the last seven months, I think there is a lot of good signs for us, it’s never going to be the exact stage we want to be at. But I thought there was really a lot of positives to take out of the game, individual, collectively as a team, senior players looking strong and fit, and the younger players doing really well.

“The spirit and the camaraderie is so important for the team, it’s great to see the boys getting on so naturally and enjoying each other’s company. Collectively we looked strong as a team, which is always the most important thing, and individual performances seeing the young players come on to have an impact.”

#1403. Yang believes Celtic can defy the odds with history-making move into the Europa League knock-out phase

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 13:39 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 13:49 EST, 22 November 2026

Yang Hyun-jun is predicting that Celtic can make Europa League history by bouncing back from a dismal start in the group stage to qualify.

Since the competition was revamped by UEFA in 2024, no side have made it through to the knock-out round having lost their first three games.

With defeats to Ferencvaros, Benfica and Celta Vigo arriving in quick succession, Martin O’Neill’s men looked to be heading for an early exit.

After beating Besiktas last time out, however, they are still in with a shout when matchday five takes them to Portugal to face Torreense on Thursday.

Winger Yang, who made his first start since early September in the win over St Mirren on Saturday, feels there’s a growing belief among the players they can yet emulate last season’s feat of reaching the play-off round.

‘Can we make history? Of course,’ he said. ‘We believe we can qualify. We are getting better all the time. You could see that against Besiktas.

Yang made his first start since early September in Celtic's victory over St Mirren on Saturday

Martin O'Neill aims to keep Celtic's Europa League hopes alive by beating Torreense this week

‘They are a very good team, and that has given us the belief that we can go to the next round. It’s important to take it game-by-game, though. This is the most important one. If we can get the points we can go on from there, step-by-step.’

Torreense made history last season by becoming the first second-tier team to win the Portuguese Cup and qualify for Europe. Despite currently sitting 13th in that division, they have confounded expectations by taking six points from four Europa League games.

‘We are playing against a Portuguese second division team but we have to be focused and aggressive,’ warned Yang. ‘They are higher than us in the Europa League table. They’ve already won two matches so they will be a good team.

‘We have to approach it the same way as we would playing a team like Benfica or Sporting Lisbon. We have to go there and try to win. If we play like we did against St Mirren, we can do it.’

Meanwhile, Yang is adamant that being made exempt from military service wasn’t even on his mind as South Korea won the Asian Games this year.

Played in Japan in September and October, Yang’s side defeated the hosts 1-0 in the final.

That meant all the South Korean players were no longer obliged to spend time serving in the military before they turn 28.

Yang, 24, who suffered a hamstring injury in the opening victory against Qatar, reflected: ‘It was great. Obviously, it was nice to win it but I also got injured, which was unfortunate.

‘I was trying to be around the team, to help in any way I could.

‘It wasn’t really about the national service. Everyone was playing for the team, the country and the fans.

‘We managed to get the victory. Being exempt from national service was just a bonus, I guess.

‘The celebrations were enjoyable. It’s the first time my national team have won the Asian Games.

‘It was really hard — especially the game against Japan. It was a great achievement.’

#1402. Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion

Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.

The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.

That goal also was supposed to set up penalties. But after minutes of waiting around – and Kevin Campello, Chelsea’s head of first-team operations, saying “it’s written in the contract” – the players walked off the pitch.

That confusion ended a feisty affair in which tensions threatened to boil over and that, at certain points, paid little attention to the “friendly” aspect of the clash with seven yellow cards shown. At one point the visitors’ new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee exchanged angry words with some of Johor’s coaching staff. The CFC TV commentary team suggested that the spot-kicks were abandoned because of the match’s heated atmosphere.

Austin MacPhee was ready to throw hands😂 pic.twitter.com/CFDgTOwmxE

Having played just 24 hours earlier in Jakarta – a 3-0 win over AC Milan – it was no surprise to see Xabi Alonso name a fresh XI, a mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters given much-needed game time.

And considering Johor are one game away from setting a new world record of 109 matches unbeaten in the top flight – a run that would surpass the current mark set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s – it was also no shock to see the Malaysian team offer a stern, pre-season test for the west Londoners.

After a good start Chelsea were second best in a first half in which Johor should have been at least two goals to the good. The Malaysian champions controlled the first 45 minutes and were 1-0 up after 14 minutes – a low cross from the left side-footed home by Arif Aiman.

The hosts gave the young, inexperienced Chelsea backline a torrid time, especially on the flanks and Óscar Arribas was guilty of not capitalising on a great chance to double Johor’s lead, his shot after cutting in from the right going wide.

While they looked vulnerable at the back, Chelsea also struggled to keep possession in attack. But they got an equaliser they scarcely deserved after Liam Delap was manhandled to the ground in the box by Kevin Medina. The striker, who may well leave Stamford Bridge before the transfer window slams shut, fired home the spot-kick allowing the visitors to go into the break on level terms.

For the most part, the second half followed a similar pattern to the first – Jofor having the better chances, while tensions on the pitch continued to run high.

It was, however, Chelsea who took the lead after the break, Delap once again scoring from the spot, this time after Jamie Gittens was brought down in the area.

Johor, though, kept on creating, thanks in part to a fairly porous visitors’ backline, and levelled through a deflected Arribas free kick, before going 3-2 up thanks thanks to a well-taken Bérgson strike.

Had it stayed that way Chelsea could have had few complaints. But as the clock approached 90 minutes, the visitors had one last attack. Mykhailo Mudryk, just on as a substitute, delivered a cross from the left that Antonio Glauder could only steer into his own net. That was supposed to set up the penalty shoot-out that did not take place and the chance for one of the sides to claim a hollow victory.

Considering a raft of changes and that fact this was far from the first XI, it is hard to know what to make of this. But among the positive things Alonso could take from the game was the impressive form of Nicolas Jackson and good centre-forward play of Delap. The negative was, however, a poor defensive display.

Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for their last pre-season friendly, against Real Sociedad, before the Premier League season starts away at local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Johor Darul Ta’zim: Syihan Hazmi; Arribas, Israfilov (Carlos Akapo 82), Medina, Antonio Glauder, Silva (La’Vere Corbin-Ong 89); Arif Aiman, Petrovic, Méndez (Nené 78), Marcos Guilherme (Bérgson); Zahedi (Stoichkov 62). Substitutes: Abad, Davies, Hidalgo, Nahuel Leiva, Lowry, Mohamadou Sumareh, Stuart Wilkin.Booked: Israfilov, Antonio Glauder, Silva.Goals: Arif Aiman (14), Arribas (65), Bérgson (86).Chelsea: Sharman-Lowe (Slolina 46); Subuloye, Adarabioyo, Anselmino (Watson 29); Geovany Quenda, Dario Essugo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Gittens (Mudryk 87); Estêvão, Delap, Jacskon (Satpaev 86). Substitutes: Curd, Diakite, Kavuma-McQueen, Sarr, Walsh.Booked: Estêvão, Delap, Jackson, Geovany Quenda, Watson.Goals: Delap (42 pen, 62 pen), Antonio Glauder (89 og).

There will NOT be a penalty shootout. No one is quite sure why.

Anyway, that was an entertaining draw, plenty of good things for Chelsea (the play of Delap and Jackson) as well as worrying signs (open and vulnerable at the back).

The commentators on CFC TV are now not so sure!

That was an entertaining pre-season friendly. There was a bit of niggle and that added to the action.

There will be penalties, apparently, if it stays the same score...

Will there be a late winner? There will be four minutes of added time.

Mudryk just on picks up the ball on the left and, with four Chelsea players in the box, crosses into the danger area. It’s a good ball and asks too many questions of the hosts as Glauder diverts the ball into his own net.

It’s what the host have, on the balance of play, deserved, but it’s a gift from Chelsea. Essugo loses the ball in the final third and Bergson, on as sub pick it put driving at the box before hitting a low shot from outside the area, the ball nestling in the left corner of the net.

Chelsea have been better this half than the first 45, they’ve been able to control the pace of the game well since the break.

The pace has slowed down since the break, Chelsea seeing more of the ball. They work it right before Watson loses possession on the edge of the area.

The referee clearly forgot about the hydration break and the two teams are having a belated one now. Delightful...

I reckon there’s another goal left in this match. It’s been entertaining fare and the hosts have given as good as they’ve got, if not more.

This has been a lively match, better than most run-of-the-mill pre-season friendlies. Chelsea seeing a fair bit of possession at the moment, can they fashion a chance?

Yes they can. But it’s a longish shot from Gittens that is easily saved by Hamzi in the JDT goal.

More niggle in this match that hasn’t really had many tough challenges. After a few handbags the referee takes control and the argy bargy peters out.

It’s the least the hosts deserve. They have a free-kick 25 yards out, Arribas takes it with his right it’s at the wall but in turning away from the ball Delap deflects it into the far-right corner giving Slonina no chance.

Fluky goal but the hosts have deserved their bit of luck.

Delap again with the goal, this time he goes low, but still to the keeper’s right.

Penalty for Chelsea. Gittens cuts back in the box onto his right and is clipped by the defender. Clear-cut penalty.

Half-chance for Delap on the edge of the area. He playes a one-two with Jackson before opening up his body and letting fly, the shot going well wide.

Another good chance for the hosts and it’s not shock to write that it’s come from the industry of Arribas on the right. He fires in a low cross that evades everyone in the box.

Estevao goes down in the box, it looks as though it could well be a penalty but the referee waves play on. The Brazilian is the shown a yellow card for possibly lashing out having not got the decision he wanted.

The hosts have asserted themselves well this half, in much the same way as they did in the first 45 minutes.

Another good chance for the hosts and again it’s all too easy as Zahedi is one-on-one with the keeper. The striker, however, dithers a bit too long and Slonina makes a fine save. JDT have had plenty of chances to add to their sole goal...

Chelsea have had a ragged start to this half.

Good work from JDT who keep the ball well in midfield before a throughball is played to the on-rushing Zahedi but Slonina comes out well.

They’re back under way in Johor, and there’s an early chance for Jackson who gets the ball in the box, but the ball gets stuck underneath him and he cannot get in a good attempt in on goal.

And that is the last action of an entertaining half. Chelsea started well before the hosts opened the scoring. JDT then took control of the half and should, if truth be told, have extended their lead. But Delap did well to earn the penalty that he subsequently scored and should have made it 2-1 with the last kick of the 45.

Worrying signs at the back, however, for Alonso. Will Chelsea go to four at the back after the break?

The answer to that question (see last post) was so very nearly yes...

Jackson plays in a peach of a through ball with the outside of his right foot, Delap is one-on-one with the keeper and looks for all the world as though he has to score. BUT he scuffs his shot wide.

There will be three minutes of added time. Can Chelsea head into the break with an unexpected lead?

Free-kick for Chelsea on the JDT byline. The ball is put deep into the box, it’s headed back by Tosin before the ball is blazed over the bar.

A minute later Tosin then let’s fly form 25 yards, the ball goes well over the bar.

The hosts should have been more than 1-0 to the good and now they’re drawing. Goals change matches...

Having won the penalty Delap fires the spotkick home, sending the keeper the the wrong way.

Penalty to Chelsea and it’s all thanks to good centre-forward play by Delap. He gets the ball in the box and Medina manhands him to the ground. The referee doesn’t hesitate before pointing to the spot.

Chelsea have struggled to create anything since the opening 15 minutes. They have no control at the front and none at the back currently.

As I type that JDT have another good chance to turn the 1-0 lead into a 2-0 lead. Arribas, whose been a menace all game, dances toward the Chelsea box before delaying the pass too long.

JDT are finding a lot of joy on the flanks, there are three at the back for Chelsea and on the outside are two youngsters. The hosts are working the space well.

Yet again Chelsea are made to look decidedly average. A simple ball over the top on the right opens up the visitors’ defence and Arribas is in on goal, he cuts in and lets fly with his left peg, the shot going wide.

That should have been 2-0 to the Malaysian powerhouses.

Worrying signs for Chelsea who have struggled to keep possession up top and looked vulnerable at the back.

Yet more good work from JDT who are being given space by Chelsea. Marcos Guilherme slaloms into the west Londoners’ box and Tosin again doesn’t look the most assured but the JDT player cuts the ball back and the visitors can clear the danger.

Another good attack from the hosts who get in a shot in on goal, it’s deflected and loops into the grateful arms of Sharman-Lowe in the Chelsea goal.

There’s a break in play with Anselmino down and suffering what looks like a hamstring injury. He is eventually replaced by Reggie Watson.

Meanwhile, the home fans are in fine voice and waving several HUGE flags.

Yep, everyone’s least favourite part of the World Cup in the U, S of A is back. To be fair it’s humid in Johor so taking on fluids during the first 45 minutes is no bad idea.

There’s a bit of argy-bargy not really what you should get in a ‘friendly’. There hasn’t been a bad chellenge in the match so far so not sure where that came from...

Yet more good work from the hosts, this time it’s down the right, Arribas getting the better of Anselmino before shooting at the near post - the attempt hitting the side netting.

After a lively start Chelsea have been second best.

Poor defending from the visitors there but the chance was well snapped up by JDT.

Lovely break from the hosts. They break down the left at pace, before the ball is threaded through to the back post and Arif Aiman sidefoots into the back of the net with aplomb.

So very nearly an opener for Chelsea. They break at pace thanks to Estevao who drives down the middle before playing in Jackson. The striker cuts in from the left and shoots, the attempt is saved well by Hamzi and Estevao’s follow up is wide. Is a goal coming?

Free-kick for Chelsea some 35 yards out. Too far fro a shot on goal? Of course it is. The ball is floated into the box and the visitors earn a corner.

What can they create from this set piece? ‘Not much’ is the initial answer as the ball is cleared by JDT but Chelsea win possession back and the ball is fed to Estevao on the left, the Brazilian goes for go with his trusty left peg but the bal goes high and wide.

JDT attack down the left, it’s a lovely ball in that forces a fine header to clear the danger from Adarabioyo.

No sooner had I sent that last post than Chelsea break through the middle. The ball is fed through to Delap who gets a left-footed shot in on goal forcing a good save from the JDT keeper Hamzi.

Quiet, low-key start to the match. No real shock there, it is a pre-season friendly.

JDT give the ball away in their half and Chelsea have a half-decent platform to launch an attack from. They cannot fashion a chance and also lose possession.

They’re under way in southern Malaysia, Chelsea are in their vibrant blue and the hosts are wearing a fetching pink number. There was a late change for the visitors, Mamadou Sarr has been replaced by Olutayo Subuloye.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE JOHOR: Sharman-Lowe; Sarr, Tosin, Anselmino; Quenda, Nicoll-Jazuli, Essugo (c), Gittens; Estevao; Jackson, Delap; subs: Slonina, Curd, Subuloye, Diakite, Watson, Mudryk, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Satpayev

...Luis Garcia. The Spaniard has history with Chelsea, remember the ‘ghost goal’?

Arriving for duty! 🫡 pic.twitter.com/M2XEkLC18n

Your Chelsea side today! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0OvvGVmgpc

A mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters you may not have heard of.

Johor Darul Ta’Zim – more commonly known as JDT – are the Man Utd of Malaysia (at least that’s according to a Malaysian friend of mine). In 2013, they were going nowhere and were the dictionary definition of a stagnant club, low on confidence and trophies. That was until the Crown Prince bought the club and, over the next 13 years, transformed it into the powerhouse it is today.

As if to underline JDT’s dominance over Malaysian football they are one game away from the world record unbeaten run in a top flight. The new season of the Malaysian Super League gets under way later this month and should they avoid defeat in their opening match they will extend their unbeaten run - which began in April 2021 - to 109 games and surpass the world record set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s.

Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”
